newsitem.title: USA: ICE HOCKEY-CANADA EDGES SWEDEN IN WORLD CUP SECOND OVERTIME.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-CANADA EDGES SWEDEN IN WORLD CUP SECOND OVERTIME.

text.p: Theoren Fleury fired in a 20-footer with just 12.5 seconds left in the second sudden-death overtime early Sunday morning to lift Canada to a 3-2 win over Sweden in ice hockey's World Cup semifinal.
Canada will play the winner of Sunday's Russia-United States contest at Ottawa in the best-of-three World Cup finals starting Tuesday in Philadelphia.
Just when it appeared the game would go to a third overtime, Canada's Paul Coffey of the Detroit Red Wings picked up a loose puck in the Swedish zone and forwarded it to Fleury, a Calgary Flame.
Fleury shot from the right faceoff circle, with the Hartford Whalers' Brendan Shanahan screening Swedish goalkeeper Tommy Salo.
Salo, a New York Islander who helped Sweden win the gold medal at the 1994 Winter Olympics, dove after the puck as it entered his net, then burst into tears.
"Paul Coffey got the puck and dropped it off to me," said Fleury. "I just tried to get it on net and fortunately it went in. This means we play another series."
"I haven't much to say as I am very disappointed," said Kent Forsberg, the Swedish coach. "It is always hard to lose a game after five periods. The better team always wins this kind of game."
"Any time you win in overtime there is some luck in it," said Canadian coach Glen Sather.
Sweden had mounted a third-period comeback on goals from Tommy Albelin and Mikael Nylander, both of the Flames, which negated two earlier Canadian goals.
Albelin beat Canadian goalkeeper Curtis Joseph with an unscreened 59-footer at 5:47 and Nylander's second rebound eluded Joseph at 13:33 to gain the deadlock.
Washington Capitals defenceman Calle Johansson assisted on both goals, leading the rush on the second score and firing the first shot, which Joseph stopped.
Mats Sundin of the Toronto Maple Leafs put another shot on net, which Joseph batted away to his left. Nylander poked at the puck twice, backhanded, and the second effort flew high into the net.
Joseph, of the Edmonton Oilers, and forward Eric Lindros of the Philadelphia Flyers had earlier given virtuoso performances as Canada took a 2-0 lead.
Joseph held Canada in the game for two periods before weakening.
He stopped 14 Swedish shots in the first period, when Canada only managed five, and stopped another 12 in the second, many of them close-in, when Canada had nine shots.
"Curtis (Joseph) was unbelievable in the first period and kept them alive," said Swedish coach Forsberg.
"This win could be the one that brings us over the top," said Joseph. "This looks like the game that will bring us together. We sure had a good workout tonight."

Lindros, criticised for poor play in the first four games, scored the first goal of the game at 17:59 of the first period. He knocked Swedish defenceman Mattias Norstrom off the puck to start the play, then rushed to the open side of the net where he converted a pass from Shanahan.
In the second period, the New York Rangers' Adam Graves hit a post in the second minute, but Sweden again pressed and tested Joseph.
Sundin clanged a shot off the left post with 15:00 left in the period. The Rangers' Niklas Sundstrom had two close-in shots that were stopped by Joseph midway through the period.
The Colorado Avalanche's Peter Forsberg almost scored on a wraparound with 10:21 left before Joseph stopped a Sundin power-play point shot in the 12th minute.
Then Lindros again picked on Norstrom, who plays with the Los Angeles Kings.

Lindros knocked him off a loose puck near the Canadian blue line and defenceman Scott Niedermayer of the New Jersey Devils skated the length of the rink, going around the Detroit Red Wings' defender Niklas Lidstrom, and beat Salo with a soft 10-foot poke.
At the end of regulation play Sweden had outshot Canada 33-23.
"Sweden had a lot of chances," said Fleury. "Part of the time they seemed to be shot out of a cannon, they came so hard."
In the first overtime Canada managed one more shot than Sweden, 8-7. The New York Rangers' Wayne Gretzky hit the post with four minutes left in the period.

In the second overtime Salo stopped the New York Rangers' Mark Messier, Fleury and Lindros in the first 10 minutes. Sweden's Johan Garpenlov, a Florida Panther, missed an open net with 1:40 left, leading to the Canadian game-winner in the ensuing play.
Both teams finished with 43 total shots.
All three European teams played just one game in North America, lost and returned home. Germany lost to Canada and Finland lost to Russia.
